questions.enonce_markdown:
Two statements $p$ and $q$ are defined as:

$p$: Kelvin will go to Kribi.

$q$: Kelvin will visit the seaport.

Translate into ordinary English, the statements:

(a) $p \Rightarrow q$

(b) $p \wedge q$

(c) $\sim p \vee \sim q$ (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Here $\Rightarrow$ is "implies" (if ... then), $\wedge$ is "and", $\vee$ is "or" and $\sim$ is "not".

**(a)** $p \Rightarrow q$: "If Kelvin goes to Kribi, then he will visit the seaport."

**(b)** $p \wedge q$: "Kelvin will go to Kribi and he will visit the seaport."

**(c)** $\sim p \vee \sim q$: "Kelvin will not go to Kribi or he will not visit the seaport" (at least one of the two fails).

By De Morgan's law, $\sim p \vee \sim q \equiv \sim(p \wedge q)$, so (c) is equivalent to "It is not the case that Kelvin will both go to Kribi and visit the seaport", the negation of statement (b).

questions.enonce_markdown: The position vectors of the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}$ and $7\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ respectively. Find the vector equation of the line $AB$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Position vectors: $\mathbf{a} = (2, -1, -3)$, $\mathbf{b} = (1, 1, -4)$, $\mathbf{c} = (7, 2, 1)$. A direction vector of $AB$ is
$$\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} = (1 - 2,\ 1 + 1,\ -4 + 3) = (-1, 2, -1).$$
The line through $A$ with this direction is $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + t\,\overrightarrow{AB}$:
$$\boxed{\mathbf{r} = (2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}) + t(-\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}), \quad t \in \mathbb{R}}$$
(equivalently, $\mathbf{r} = (2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}) + s(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})$; in Cartesian form $\dfrac{x - 2}{-1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{2} = \dfrac{z + 3}{-1}$).

Check: $t = 0$ gives $A$ and $t = 1$ gives $(1, 1, -4) = B$.

questions.enonce_markdown: The position vectors of the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}$ and $7\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ respectively. Find the Cartesian equation of the plane $ABC$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Two vectors in the plane: $\overrightarrow{AB} = (-1, 2, -1)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a} = (7 - 2,\ 2 + 1,\ 1 + 3) = (5, 3, 4)$. A normal vector is their vector product:
$$\mathbf{n} = \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = (8 + 3)\mathbf{i} - (-4 + 5)\mathbf{j} + (-3 - 10)\mathbf{k} = 11\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 13\mathbf{k}.$$
The plane is $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}$, with $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 2(11) + (-1)(-1) + (-3)(-13) = 22 + 1 + 39 = 62$:
$$\boxed{11x - y - 13z = 62}$$
Check with the other two points: $B(1, 1, -4)$: $11 - 1 + 52 = 62$; $C(7, 2, 1)$: $77 - 2 - 13 = 62$.

questions.enonce_markdown: The position vectors of the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}$ and $7\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ respectively. Find the sine of the angle between the line $AB$ and the plane $ABC$. (8 marks for part (ii), (a), (b) and (c) together)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method.** If a line has direction vector $\mathbf{d}$ and a plane has normal vector $\mathbf{n}$, the angle $\theta$ between the line and the plane satisfies
$$\sin\theta = \frac{|\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}|}{|\mathbf{d}|\,|\mathbf{n}|}.$$

**Application as printed.** Here $\mathbf{d} = \overrightarrow{AB} = (-1, 2, -1)$ and $\mathbf{n} = (11, -1, -13)$ from part (b):
$$\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n} = (-1)(11) + (2)(-1) + (-1)(-13) = -11 - 2 + 13 = 0.$$
So
$$\sin\theta = \frac{0}{\sqrt6\,\sqrt{291}} = 0.$$
$$\boxed{\sin\theta = 0 \quad (\theta = 0)}$$

**Interpretation.** The line $AB$ joins two of the three points that define the plane $ABC$, so it lies **in** the plane: it is perpendicular to the normal ($\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 0$) and the angle between the line and the plane is $0$. (Printed-question note: the question as printed therefore has the trivial answer $0$. For a line that is not contained in the plane, with direction $\mathbf{d}$, the same formula applies with $|\mathbf{n}| = \sqrt{11^2 + 1^2 + 13^2} = \sqrt{291}$.)
